title: How do you read a profit and loss statement in a case interview?
description: A simple walk through a profit and loss statement (income statement): revenue, gross margin, operating costs, EBITDA and net profit, and how they appear in…
hook: Some cases hand you a simplified profit and loss statement, and if you have never read one, it can look like a wall of numbers. It is really just a story told from top to bottom: money comes in, costs come out in layers, and what is left is profit. Here is how to read it in a minute.
body:
From top to bottom

  1. Revenue (also called sales or turnover): all the money earned from customers.
  2. Cost of goods sold: the direct cost of making or buying what was sold, such as materials and factory labour.
  3. Gross profit = revenue − cost of goods sold. Divided by revenue, it gives the gross margin.
  4. Operating costs: the costs of running the business, such as sales and marketing, head office, rent and IT.
  5. EBITDA: profit before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation. A rough measure of operating cash profit, often used to value companies.
  6. Depreciation and amortisation: spreading the cost of long-lasting assets, like machines, over their useful life.
  7. Operating profit (EBIT), then interest and tax, and finally net profit.

How to read one quickly in a case

  • Turn every line into a percentage of revenue. Changes in percentages show what is really moving.
  • Compare years side by side, and with competitors if you have them.
  • Look for the line that grew faster than revenue. That is usually where the story is.

An example

Revenue grew from £100M to £110M, but operating profit fell from £12M to £8M. Cost of goods stayed at 60% of revenue, so gross profit rose by £4M. Other costs were flat, but marketing jumped from £8M (8% of revenue) to £16M (about 14.5%). That extra £8M of marketing more than wiped out the £4M gain, so the profit fall is all marketing spend. The next question: did that marketing bring in customers who will pay off later, or was it wasted?

A phrase to use

Let me put each line as a share of revenue so I can see which cost has grown faster than sales.

Follow a simple income statement all the way down

Imagine a manufacturer with £100 million of revenue, £60 million cost of goods sold, £20 million operating expenses that exclude depreciation, and £5 million depreciation and amortisation. Gross profit is £40 million, EBITDA is £20 million, and operating income (EBIT) is £15 million. If interest costs £3 million and income tax is £3 million, net profit is £9 million, assuming no other items.

The timing of investment matters. If the company buys a £30 million machine with a ten-year useful life, the £30 million is generally capitalised as an asset rather than expensed entirely through the income statement on day one. Straight-line depreciation would be £3 million per year before considering residual value. Actual cash outflow and accounting profit are therefore different. Depreciation reduces EBIT, while the capital purchase appears in investing cash flows.

When diagnosing declining profit, compare each line as a share of revenue and examine whether the change reflects price, volume, product mix or cost inflation. Do not automatically treat EBITDA as cash flow: working capital, capital investment, interest and tax can all matter. In a case, ask which profit definition the client wants to improve.
